newsitem.title: USA: GM launches company-wide certification program.
newsitem.headline: GM launches company-wide certification program.

text.p: General Motors Corp., looking for an edge in the increasingly competitive used car business, is launching a new company-wide effort to market its used cars under the GM brand name and boost sales by its dealers.

In an updated and expanded version of its "OK Used Cars" promotional effort from the 1960s, selected GM dealers will offer "GM Certified Used Vehicles." Advertising for the new brand programme is expected to start Wednesday.

Unlike the previous programme, the new programme will take extensive steps to ensure that GM's cars and trucks are free from defect, including inspections, reconditioning and warranties. Dealers also said vehicles under the programme will be sold at no-haggle prices.
Individual GM divisions currently offer their own used vehicle certification programmes, but the new programme is the first such company-wide effort.

It also is GM's second major effort in recent months to emphasise the GM brand name over the company's divisional brands. Last December, GM began marketing its EV1 electric car under the GM nameplate.

About 500 of GM's more than 8,000 U.S. dealers have signed up for the programme so far. One of them, Jim Butler, a St. Louis-area Chevrolet and Saturn dealer, has opened a stand-alone store to sell the used vehicles.

"This is no longer a pilot programme, it's full throttle," said Rick Strifler, general sales manager at Jim Butler GM Certified Used Vehicles in Crestwood, Mo. "It's actually a whole new brand that they're going to support with advertising."

Analysts said the effort will allow GM dealers to better compete with the growing used-car superstore chains, such as entrepreneur Wayne Huizenga's AutoNation USA and Circuit City Stores Inc.'s CarMax.
Art Spinella, managing director of CNW Marketing Research in Bandon, Ore., said he thought GM has an advantage by offering used-car warranties that can be honoured throughout its dealership network.
He said the effort was a sign of the growing attention automakers are giving to the used car business.
"Manufacturers have recognised that they have to be in the used car business," he said. "They have to sop up all of those used cars that are coming off leases."

The growth of leasing has created a glut of 2- and 3-year-old cars that are attractive to people who would have bought new cars. GM could bring some of those buyers back to its dealerships with the new certification programmes, said Chris Cedergren, a consultant with Nextrend in Thousand Oaks, Calif.
The programme also could help GM offer lower monthly lease payments on new cars and trucks by propping up resale values that are used to calculate lease payments.
